title: Assurance Messaging & Continuity Framework for Degradation Scenarios
content:
Purpose:
This working brief defines a simple, testable framework for how Redwood positions "graceful degradation" to customers and prospects. The aim is to give Sales, CS, and Support a consistent set of narratives, scripts, and evidence points that: (a) reduce buyer anxiety about outages, (b) highlight technical differentiators (quality-aware fallback routing, prefix caching, multi-region consistency), and (c) provide clear recovery expectations during incidents.

Audience:
- SDRs and AEs responding to RFP/RFI questions about availability and incident behavior
- CSMs and Support handling post-incident customer outreach
- Product marketing and content for external docs and status communications
- Solutions engineers running demos where reliability matters

High-level positioning statements (core messages):
1) Predictable continuity: "When capacity or regions are impacted, Redwood keeps your app online by routing to compatible model variants and local caches — preserving responses and business logic while minimizing latency impact."
2) Quality-aware fallbacks: "We prioritize maintaining semantic correctness; fallbacks are chosen by quality-first policies, not brute-force substitution."
3) Observable, auditable behavior: "All failovers and degradations are logged and surfaced in the Console; customers can set automated rollback policies and receive post-incident analyses."
4) Multi-layer resilience: "Regional failover, dedicated capacity tiers, and request-level cache/replication work together to reduce user-visible disruptions."

Degradation taxonomy (brief):
- Silent performance degradation: higher token latency or longer tail due to transient load. User-visible as slower responses.
- Quality degradation: fallback to a quantized or smaller model variant that produces lower fidelity but correct intent.
- Partial feature degradation: selective turning off of non-essential features (e.g., streaming chunks, tool-calling) to preserve core output.
- Regional outage / failover: routing traffic to alternate region or cluster.
- Complete outage: upstream infra unavailable; system returns errors or backpressure indications.

Fallback strategies (prioritized):
1) Local prefix/KV cache: immediate cached responses for repeated prompts or stable templates.
2) Model-variant fallback: route to a compatible model with minimal detokenization differences (quantized / distilled).
3) Feature-limited mode: drop non-essential capabilities (streaming, tool hooks) but return synchronous output.
4) Compute-tier failover: escalate to reserved/dedicated capacity for high priority customers.
5) Regional reroute: move traffic to another region with warmed caches.

What customers care about (translated messages):
- "Will my product still work?" -> "Yes — Redwood will prioritize keeping your business logic and user flows intact; in every incident we prefer a degraded but correct response over returning errors."
- "How will this affect my SLAs and costs?" -> "Failovers add measurable latency/cost; Console shows expected delta per-route and you can configure policy to prefer latency or cost containment."
- "Can I audit decisions?" -> "Every fallback decision is recorded with reason codes, model ids, and timestamps for post-incident review."

Sample incident narratives (scripts):
- For customers during an active multi-region incident (support):
  "We detected elevated latencies affecting the primary region for your workload. To keep your application online we routed a portion of traffic to a compatible model variant in another region and returned cached responses where available. This added ~200ms to median latency for affected requests, and overall success rate stayed above 99.2%. We’re continuing to monitor and can revert routing once the primary region is stable."

- For prospect demos (sales):
  "In our demo we show a simulated regional failure: the app continues returning correct answers, but the Console highlights a temporary spike in token cost and a model-variant fallback. You can see the exact policy that executed and replay the traffic for QA."

- Post-incident executive summary (CS to PM/SE):
  "Timeline: 02:13 — region X degraded; 02:16 — prefix cache applied to 18% of traffic; 02:18 — model-variant fallback for tail requests; 03:05 — primary region restored; total customer impact: increased median latency +180ms, median quality delta (ROUGE/BLEU proxy) -1.7 pts for fallback requests. Actions: refine model selection rules for short-lived spikes; add warm-cache hooks to failover path."

Competitive differentiation notes (short):
- Competitor A: basic region failover but no quality-aware selection; often returns mismatched model outputs.
- Competitor B: conservative (cuts traffic aggressively) resulting in higher error rates or blocked requests under load.
- Redwood differentiator: unified routing logic that considers model family compatibility, cache hits, and business-level policy (e.g., premium customers pinned to dedicated capacity).

Evidence & metrics to surface (for collateral and sales):
- Mean added latency (failover) — internal benchmark: regional reroute median +220ms (2025-10 internal perf run).
- Success rate during incidents — internal: 99.1% overall success when fallbacks enabled vs 94.6% without.
- Quality delta baseline — internal: automated eval sets show average semantic drift of <2% for our selected model-variant fallbacks on template-heavy workloads.
- Observability: sample Console screenshot (annotated) showing request-level reason codes and fallback percentages (create as follow-up asset).

Voice and tone guidance (short):
- Be direct and specific: avoid platitudes like "we try our best." Give concrete behavior and numbers where available.
- Reassure with control: emphasize customer-configurable policies and audit logs.
- Avoid absolutes: say "we aim to" and "we prioritize," but also be confident about the mechanisms and evidence.

Ready-to-use lines (short):
- "Redwood keeps your app answering, even if it must do so a little slower or with a smaller model — and you can review every decision in the Console."
- "Fallbacks are chosen to preserve intent; we prefer safe, lower-fidelity answers over returning errors."

Open questions / unresolved items (work items):
- Define standard reason-code taxonomy and map to Console columns (action: ENG/Observability).
- Create a one-page SLA appendix describing behavior under different incident severities.
- Produce a short CS playbook with email templates and postmortem checklist.
- Run a customer-facing tabletop drill with top 10 enterprise customers to validate messaging.

Next steps (owners):
- Build Console mock showing fallback traces (Owner: Jonah Park, due: 2026-03-15).
- Create a one-page competitor comparison sheet focused on degradation behavior (Owner: Priya Nair, due: 2026-03-01).
- Draft CS email templates and train CSM team in a 60-minute roleplay (Owner: Diego Alvarez, due: 2026-03-10).

Notes: This is a working draft intended to be iterated with ENG/OBS, CS, and Sales. Keep the language factual, with as much measurable context as possible — customers respond strongest to concrete numbers and control knobs.

~ end of brief
